goldenPoints: Schneider's first-rank symptoms: thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcast, passivity, voices commenting or arguing, delusional perception
Acute dystonia on haloperidol → IV/IM anticholinergic (benzatropine or promethazine) immediately
Delirium tremens appears 48–72 hours after stopping alcohol; benzodiazepines are the treatment
Lithium in pregnancy → Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist — the atypical with the least metabolic and prolactin trouble
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + raised CPK — stop the antipsychotic
Clozapine is for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and can cause agranulocytosis — monitor blood counts
Depression is linked to low serotonin and noradrenaline; SSRIs are first-line drugs, CBT first for mild depression
Capgras syndrome: a familiar person is believed replaced by an identical imposter
Rett syndrome: a girl who develops normally, then regresses with hand-wringing stereotypies
intro: Psychiatry carries 5 questions per FMGE paper, drawn from a small, very repeatable pool: first-rank symptoms, delusion types, antipsychotic side effects and their antidotes, alcohol withdrawal timing, and childhood disorders. Stems are short vignettes — learn to map each vignette phrase to its named phenomenon.
subject: Psychiatry
tagline: FMGE asks named phenomena — first-rank symptoms, delusion types, drug side effects and withdrawal timings

topics.askedAs: name the phenomenon in the vignette
topics.oneLiner: Passivity = 'my thoughts/actions are controlled from outside'; Capgras = imposter; erotomania = 'he loves me' without evidence.
points: A delusion is a fixed, false, unshakable belief, out of keeping with the person's culture and education
A hallucination is a perception without a stimulus; an illusion is a misinterpretation of a real stimulus
Pseudohallucination: experienced in inner subjective space, with insight retained — the patient knows it is not real perception

Schneider's first-rank symptoms: thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting; passivity phenomena (made acts, feelings, impulses); voices commenting or arguing; audible thoughts; delusional perception
Passivity phenomenon: the patient believes his thoughts, feelings or actions are controlled by an external agency
Capgras syndrome: a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an identical-looking imposter
De Clerambault syndrome (erotomania): the false belief that another person, usually of higher status, is in love with the patient
Persecutory (paranoid) delusions are the commonest type of delusion overall
Flat (blunted) affect — poverty of emotional expression — is a negative symptom, seen in schizophrenia
Formication is a tactile hallucination of insects crawling on the skin, classic in cocaine use and delirium tremens
Sudden confusion with hallucinations hours after surgery or in a sick patient is delirium until proved otherwise: acute onset, fluctuating course, disorientation
topics.title: Basics & Psychopathology: Delusions, Hallucinations, Defence Mechanisms
topics.trap: Pseudohallucination is NOT a 'false hallucination' to dismiss — its defining features are inner-space location and preserved insight.

topics.oneLiner: Third-person auditory hallucinations + first-rank symptoms + a young patient = schizophrenia; disorganised (hebephrenic) type fares worst.
points: Bleuler's four As: autism (withdrawal), ambivalence, affective blunting, and loosening of associations
Auditory hallucinations are the commonest hallucinations in schizophrenia; third-person and running-commentary voices are characteristic
Negative symptoms (the 5 As of deficit): alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality and affective flattening
Catatonic features: stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing and waxy flexibility
Disorganised (hebephrenic) schizophrenia has the worst prognosis; paranoid schizophrenia the relatively best among classic subtypes
Good prognostic factors: acute onset, late onset, obvious precipitating stress, affective symptoms, female sex, good premorbid adjustment
Treatment rests on dopamine D2-blocking antipsychotics; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness
Delusional disorder: a single, non-bizarre delusion with otherwise preserved personality and functioning
Schizophrenia typically begins in late adolescence or early adult life
topics.title: Schizophrenia & Other Psychotic Disorders
topics.trap: Voices discussing the patient in the third person are a first-rank symptom — do not label every auditory hallucination in a vignette as 'just schizophrenia' without checking for delirium or mood disorder with psychotic features.

topics.askedAs: diagnosis from symptom cluster; first drug/class
topics.oneLiner: Low mood + anhedonia + early-morning waking for over 2 weeks = depression; think serotonin and noradrenaline.
points: Core symptoms of depression: persistently low mood, anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure) and fatigability, lasting at least 2 weeks
Biological features: early-morning awakening, appetite and weight loss, loss of libido, psychomotor retardation, mood worst in the morning
Depression is classically linked to reduced serotonin and noradrenaline activity
Beck's cognitive triad: negative views of the self, the world and the future
Recurrent depressive disorder means two or more separate depressive episodes
Mild depression: psychological treatment (CBT) is the recommended first step before antidepressants
SSRIs are the first-line drug class for moderate–severe depression
Tricyclics are dangerous in overdose (cardiotoxicity) and strongly anticholinergic; MAO inhibitors can trigger a tyramine ('cheese') hypertensive crisis
Atypical depression shows hypersomnia, increased appetite and mood reactivity
Postpartum blues are mild and self-limiting in days; postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency
topics.title: Depression & Antidepressants
topics.trap: A depressed patient who suddenly becomes energetic in the first weeks of treatment carries a high suicide risk — energy returns before mood lifts.

topics.askedAs: mood stabiliser choice; lithium in pregnancy
topics.oneLiner: Decreased NEED for sleep separates mania from mere insomnia; lithium's fetal signature is Ebstein anomaly.
points: Mania: elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy for at least 1 week, causing marked impairment
Signature manic features: decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, distractibility and reckless spending
Hypomania is the same picture in milder form for at least 4 days, without psychosis or marked impairment
Lithium is the classic first-line mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder and for mania prophylaxis
Lithium in pregnancy is associated with Ebstein anomaly — downward displacement of the tricuspid valve
Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index; toxicity gives coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion
Long-term lithium effects: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia (fatigue, constipation, stones, polyuria)
Valproate in pregnancy is linked to neural tube defects; it is avoided in women of childbearing age where possible
Rapid cycling bipolar disorder means four or more mood episodes in a year
topics.title: Mania, Bipolar Disorder & Mood Stabilisers
topics.trap: Polyuria, constipation, stones and low mood in a patient on lithium point to hypercalcaemia from hyperparathyroidism — check calcium before blaming the depression.

topics.askedAs: which side effect, and its immediate treatment
topics.oneLiner: Dystonia in hours, parkinsonism in weeks, dyskinesia in years — and rigidity with fever is NMS until proved otherwise.
points: Extrapyramidal side effects follow a time order: acute dystonia (hours–days) → akathisia → drug-induced parkinsonism (days–weeks) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years)
Acute dystonia on haloperidol: treat immediately with an IV/IM anticholinergic such as benzatropine or promethazine

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, high fever, autonomic instability and raised CPK — stop the antipsychotic at once and give supportive care (dantrolene/bromocriptine are the named drugs)
Haloperidol is a potent typical antipsychotic with high EPS risk and QT prolongation
Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so regular blood-count monitoring is mandatory
Aripiprazole is a dopamine D2 partial agonist — it has the least metabolic disturbance and minimal prolactin rise among atypicals
Risperidone raises prolactin the most among commonly used atypicals
Olanzapine and clozapine cause the most weight gain and metabolic syndrome
Anticholinergics used for drug-induced parkinsonism (e.g. trihexyphenidyl) themselves cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and urinary retention
topics.title: Antipsychotics & Their Side Effects
topics.trap: Anticholinergics help dystonia and parkinsonism but WORSEN tardive dyskinesia — timing of the movement disorder decides the treatment.

topics.askedAs: match the anxiety syndrome to the vignette
topics.oneLiner: Worry about everything for years = GAD; a 10-minute surge of doom = panic; a feared object = phobia — name the phobia by its object.
points: Generalised anxiety disorder: excessive, hard-to-control worry about many everyday things for at least 6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, muscle tension and disturbed sleep
A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear peaking within minutes: palpitations, sweating, choking sensation, chest pain and fear of dying
Panic disorder treatment: SSRIs plus cognitive behavioural therapy; benzodiazepines only short term
Acrophobia is fear of heights; other named phobias: claustrophobia (closed spaces), agoraphobia (crowds/open places, fear of being trapped), social anxiety disorder (scrutiny by others)
Specific phobias are treated by exposure-based therapy (systematic desensitisation)
Adjustment disorder: emotional/behavioural symptoms arising within about 3 months of an identifiable stressor, out of proportion but below the threshold of a major disorder
Anxiety symptoms can be secondary — always think of hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma and substance withdrawal in a vignette
topics.title: Anxiety Disorders, Panic & Phobias
topics.trap: A first 'panic attack' in an older patient with chest pain is a medical emergency first — rule out cardiac causes before calling it panic disorder.

topics.askedAs: OCD vs conversion vs fugue vignettes
topics.oneLiner: Intrusive thought + ritual = OCD; a lost function with a calm patient = conversion; travel + lost identity = fugue.
points: Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts; compulsions are rituals performed to neutralise them
Contamination fears with repeated hand-washing are the commonest OCD presentation
OCD treatment: SSRIs (often at higher doses) and CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP); clomipramine is the classic alternative drug
Conversion (functional neurological) disorder: loss of a neurological function (e.g. aphonia, paralysis) with no organic lesion, often with la belle indifférence — a striking lack of concern
Dissociative fugue: sudden travel away from home with amnesia for one's identity, usually after severe trauma or stress
Somatisation disorder: many physical complaints across systems over years, with repeated medical consultations and no adequate organic cause
Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis): preoccupation with having a serious disease despite normal investigations and reassurance
Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect that others barely notice
topics.title: OCD, Conversion & Dissociative Disorders
topics.trap: OCD thoughts are ego-DYSTONIC (the patient knows they are senseless); the fixed beliefs of psychosis are ego-syntonic — that distinction is the favourite discriminator.

topics.askedAs: withdrawal day-count; DT features and treatment
topics.oneLiner: Tremor first, fits next, delirium tremens at 48–72 hours — benzodiazepines treat all of it; thiamine before glucose, always.
points: Alcohol withdrawal timeline: tremulousness and anxiety within 6–12 hours; withdrawal seizures at 12–48 hours; delirium tremens at 48–72 hours
The earliest (initial) sign of alcohol withdrawal is tremor, with sweating and anxiety
Delirium tremens: global confusion, disorientation, vivid visual hallucinations (animals, insects), fever and autonomic hyperactivity — it can kill if untreated
Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal and delirium tremens; lorazepam is preferred in liver disease
Wernicke's encephalopathy triad: ophthalmoplegia, gait ataxia and confusion — caused by thiamine deficiency
Give thiamine BEFORE glucose in a malnourished alcoholic, or glucose alone can precipitate Wernicke's
Korsakoff's syndrome: severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation, after Wernicke's
Formication — insects crawling on the skin — is seen in delirium tremens and in cocaine use
Relapse-prevention drugs: disulfiram (aversive), naltrexone and acamprosate
Jet-black discoloration of the tongue with tactile hallucinations is a classic cocaine-abuse picture
topics.title: Alcohol & Substance Use Disorders
topics.trap: Hallucinations at 72 hours with confusion and fever are delirium tremens, not 'alcoholic hallucinosis' — hallucinosis has a clear sensorium and appears earlier.

topics.askedAs: name the childhood disorder; IQ band
topics.oneLiner: Hand-wringing girl = Rett; long face + big ears + macroorchidism = Fragile X; binge–purge at normal weight = bulimia.
points: ADHD: inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity beginning before 12 years and present in more than one setting; first-line drug is methylphenidate, with atomoxetine as the non-stimulant option
Autism spectrum disorder: persistent deficits in social communication plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour
Rett syndrome: girls who develop normally for the first months, then regress — losing speech and hand skills, with hand-wringing stereotypies and microcephaly
Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability: long face, large ears, macroorchidism; a CGG trinucleotide repeat disorder
IQ bands: mild intellectual disability 50–69, moderate 35–49, severe 20–34, profound below 20 — an IQ of 45 is moderate
Specific learning disorder affects one domain (e.g. dyscalculia — mathematics) despite normal overall intelligence and schooling
Bulimia nervosa: recurrent binge eating with compensatory vomiting or laxatives, at a NORMAL body weight; repeated vomiting causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Anorexia nervosa: significantly low weight, intense fear of fatness, body-image distortion, amenorrhoea, lanugo hair and bradycardia
Conduct disorder: a repetitive pattern of violating others' rights and social norms; oppositional defiant disorder lacks the rights-violating aggression
topics.title: Child Psychiatry & Eating Disorders
topics.trap: Bulimia patients are usually normal weight — a low BMI with binge–purge behaviour points to the binge–purge subtype of anorexia nervosa instead.
